findings.title: Divine names as address
findings.claim: The focus's bound noun for name, followed by Allah and the two mercy epithets, can function as an act of calling upon God through those names: 17:110 names Allah and al-Rahman as callable names of one referent, while 7:180 and 73:8 connect God's names to invocation and remembrance; 59:22 identifies Allah as al-Rahman and al-Rahim.
findings.mechanism: The focus binds the word for name to Allah and apposes the mercy titles. The separate call and remembrance formulations make that named relation addressive, and the supplied identity statement places both mercy titles with Allah. The focus's two epithets can therefore be heard as names through which the opening calls on God.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader hears the formula as calling on Allah through the mercy names, with the named titles carrying how the opening addresses him.
findings.containment: The ordinary reading remains an opening in Allah's name, the Merciful, the Compassionate. This adds an address function without filling the compressed governing act, choosing one exclusive name, or treating the names as an exhaustive list.

epistemic.reason: The focus and supplied target Arabic directly connect the name phrase to calling and remembrance. Target morphology and explicit source-trust labels are absent, so the claim stays at the supplied surface and contextual relation.

findings.title: The divine name and human naming
findings.claim: The focus's phrase 'in the name of Allah' can be heard beside 12:40's distinction between names people assign to rival objects of worship without divine warrant and the rule and worship that belong to Allah alone. This gives the focus's singular divine name a bounded force of authoritative designation.
findings.mechanism: The focus binds the name to Allah; 12:40 supplies an independent act of human naming, denies those names authority, then places rule with Allah and directs worship only to him. Their contact makes the focus's naming an affirmation of the authoritative divine referent in a context where humanly assigned deity-names are explicitly challenged.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can perceive the opening's named referent as a point of allegiance, with the supplied contrast to humanly assigned deity-names clarifying what that designation carries.
findings.containment: This is a contextual boundary supplied by 12:40; the focus itself does not state an anti-idol argument or establish the history or revelation of each name. The reciprocal counter-note says the divine name alone adds no specific clarification, so this finding depends on the whole name phrase meeting 12:40's naming, authority, and worship relation.

epistemic.reason: 12:40 directly supplies the human-naming and exclusive-worship contrast, but its reciprocal counter-note limits the link and the inference is not stated by the focus itself. The packet supplies no explicit trust labels or target morphology.

findings.title: A formula at the threshold of an act
findings.claim: The focus's bound 'in the name' phrase can be heard as a threshold that accompanies what follows: 27:30 places the same full formula at the head of Solomon's message, and 11:41 uses it as Noah calls people to board and names the ark's course and anchoring.
findings.mechanism: The focus's preposition and bound noun leave the governing act compressed. In 27:30 the formula precedes a dispatched message; in 11:41 it accompanies boarding and the ark's movement. These independent uses return the focus's name phrase as an opening act that frames speech or action under Allah's name.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can experience the prefatory formula as something being done at the threshold of the next utterance or deed.
findings.containment: The supplied parallels show a framing use for the formula; they do not restore one governing verb for 92:0 or establish a single speaker-intent for every occurrence.

epistemic.reason: Both supplied target texts show the formula in a concrete message or action setting. The transfer of that framing function to 92:0 is a contextual inference, and target morphology and explicit trust labels are absent.

findings.title: Mercy as a self-assumed path of return
findings.claim: The focus's paired mercy epithets can carry an active commitment: 6:12 and 6:54 say that Allah or the Lord writes mercy upon himself, while 6:54 and 2:37 place the Merciful title in contexts of repentance and return. Together they make the named mercy legible as self-assumed care that meets a return, not only as an abstract quality.
findings.mechanism: The two focus epithets carry the mercy relation; the separate self-prescription clauses in 6:12 and 6:54 give that relation an explicit divine commitment, and the repentance-and-return scenes in 6:54 and 2:37 show the relation taking effect when a person turns back. The focus names thereby meet both commitment and enacted reception.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can hear the opening's mercy names as an active relation with a path for repentance and repair already visible elsewhere in the supplied text.
findings.containment: This does not promise automatic pardon, erase the stated turning and repair, or reduce every use of mercy to forgiveness. The interpretation of writing mercy upon himself as self-commitment remains a contextual reading of the supplied wording.

epistemic.reason: The focus and targets share explicit mercy wording, and the targets directly state self-prescription and repentance. The integrated commitment-and-return reading is an inference from their relation; no explicit trust labels or target morphology are supplied.

findings.title: The Merciful as refuge and object of trust
findings.claim: The focus's al-Rahman epithet can also be heard as naming the one sought for refuge and relied upon: 19:18 explicitly seeks refuge in al-Rahman, 36:23 places protection under his will, and 67:29 joins his name with belief and reliance.
findings.mechanism: The focus carries the divine mercy title. In 19:18 a speaker takes refuge with that title's referent; 36:23 says rival deities cannot save if al-Rahman wills harm; and 67:29 states belief in and reliance on al-Rahman. These separate refuge and trust acts return through the focus's named Merciful and make its mercy a relation of dependence and shelter.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can perceive al-Rahman in the opening as the one to whom protection and trust are directed, while the supplied contexts keep that reliance subject to his will.
findings.containment: This is a wider relation carried by al-Rahman; it does not promise immunity from harm, and it leaves the focus's primary mercy meaning intact.

epistemic.reason: The target texts explicitly attach refuge, protection, and reliance to al-Rahman. Their application to the focus's opening is a contextual extension, and no target morphology or explicit trust labels are supplied.

findings.title: Mercy held with reverence
findings.claim: The focus's al-Rahman can be heard alongside reverential fear: 36:11 and 50:33 describe people who fear al-Rahman in the unseen. The same name that carries mercy can therefore meet the reader as an object of awe and answerability.
findings.mechanism: The focus supplies the divine mercy title; the separate acts of fearing al-Rahman in 36:11 and 50:33 create a relation of reverence to the same named referent. That relation makes the opening's mercy address carry moral seriousness together with tenderness.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can hold the mercy names without flattening them into reassurance: the Merciful is also approached with reverence and responsibility.
findings.containment: Fear does not replace mercy or turn the focus into a threat. The finding preserves the distinct response recorded in the wider contexts alongside the focus's plain mercy naming.

epistemic.reason: Both supplied target texts explicitly make al-Rahman the object of fear in the unseen. Their effect on the focus is a contextual relation, not a different lexical gloss; no target morphology or explicit trust labels are supplied.

findings.title: The mercy names as source of revelation
findings.claim: The focus's paired al-Rahman and al-Rahim also name the source from whom revelation descends: 41:2 explicitly describes the sending-down as from those same two names. At the opening of a surah, the formula can therefore identify the named source of the word that follows.
findings.mechanism: The focus places both mercy titles with Allah; 41:2 independently puts both titles after a phrase naming revelation's descent from them. The repeated pair meets the distinct source relation and makes the focus's invocation point toward the origin of revealed speech.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can hear the opening's two mercy names as identifying both the one invoked and the source from whom the revealed address comes.
findings.containment: The focus itself says 'in the name of' and does not state a descent relation. The supplied parallel adds that relation without establishing which governing act is compressed in 92:0 or making a wider claim about revelation beyond the cited wording.

epistemic.reason: 41:2 directly pairs the focus's exact two epithets with a descent-from relation. Applying that source relation to the prefatory focus is a contextual inference; the packet supplies no target morphology or explicit trust labels.
